transcript.text: My Dyson V10 Absolute (SV12) won't run at all now. On the battery display there's a red light flashing when I press the trigger, then nothing. It was charging overnight. Do I need a new battery or is the whole thing dead?

A red flashing light when you pull the trigger usually points to the battery (or the charge reaching it), not the motor. The rest of the machine is probably fine. Before buying anything, though, it's worth spending 10 minutes ruling out the cheaper causes.

## Quick checks first

1. Is it actually charging?
• Plug the charger directly into the vacuum (skip the wall dock if you use one) and watch the battery LEDs. You should see blue lights pulsing or filling up.
• No lights at all suggests the charger, wall socket, or charging port. Try another outlet and check the charger's connector and the port for dust, bent pins, or damage.
• Flashing red while charging usually indicates a battery or charging fault.
• Solid amber or red while charging means the battery is too hot or too cold. If it's been in a cold garage or a hot spot, let it reach room temperature (~5–35°C) and try again.

2. Reset the charger
Unplug the charger from the wall for about a minute, plug it back in, and recharge for a few hours.

3. Check the dock contacts (if you charge on the dock)
Make sure the vacuum is sitting fully on the dock and the contacts are clean.

4. Rule out a blockage or filter issue
This usually causes pulsing (on/off/on/off) rather than a red light, but it's quick to check. Remove and inspect the rear filter, empty the bin, and check the wand and cleaner head for clogs.

## If none of that helps

If the charger shows signs of life but you still get the red flash on the trigger, the battery has most likely failed. This is very common on V10s after a few years of use. The good news:

• Replacement batteries are available from Dyson directly and third-party sellers. Genuine Dyson batteries cost more but are generally safer and more reliable. Cheap third-party lithium packs vary a lot in quality.
• The V10 battery is held in by screws (usually Torx/star screws on the handle area), so you'll need a screwdriver. It's a straightforward DIY swap.
• Order the correct part. Make sure it's listed for the V10 / SV12, since V11 and V8 batteries are not interchangeable.

## Warranty

If the vacuum is still within warranty (Dyson typically offers 2 years on cordless models; check your registration), contact Dyson before buying anything. They'll often replace a faulty battery for free, and their support team can confirm the fault code over the phone or chat.

If you tell me exactly what the lights do when it's plugged in to charge, I can help narrow it down further.

Charging on the charger directly, the blue lights come on, then it sometimes shows the flashing red too. Tried a different socket and the charger light is on. It's about 4.5 years old so out of guarantee, and the battery is not swollen, hot or smelly. Runtime had dropped to about 8 minutes on the lowest mode before it died.

That combination points pretty clearly to a worn-out battery, not a dead vacuum:

• 8 minutes on low is a huge drop. A healthy V10 gives up to about 60 minutes in its lowest mode, so the cells had lost most of their capacity.
• Red flashing during charging is the battery's management system flagging a fault, typically because one or more cells have degraded or fallen out of balance.
• Charger working normally (wall light on, blue LEDs appear) rules out the charger and socket.
• 4.5 years is about the typical lifespan for these packs with regular use.

The motor and the rest of the machine are very likely fine, so a new battery should bring it back to life for much less than a new vacuum.

## Getting the right battery

• Your SV12 takes the V10 battery. Check the part number on your old pack (on the battery itself, visible once removed) and match it when ordering. Dyson's site also lets you search by model or serial number, which is the safest way to confirm.
• Genuine Dyson costs more but comes with a warranty and proper cell quality. Since Dyson batteries are lithium-ion packs drawing high current, this is one part where the quality difference matters.
• If you go third-party, stick to well-reviewed sellers offering a warranty, and be wary of very cheap packs or inflated capacity claims.

## Swapping it

1. Remove the bin, wand, and any attachments.
2. Undo the Torx screws holding the battery to the handle (usually a couple; a T15 bit typically fits, but check before you start).
3. Slide or pull the battery out and fit the new one, then screw it back in.
4. Fully charge it before first use. It should show solid blue lights when done.

It takes about 5–10 minutes.

## Afterwards

• Recycle the old battery properly. Don't put it in household waste, as lithium batteries can cause fires in bin lorries. Most supermarkets, electrical retailers, and local recycling centres accept them.
• With the new battery, you should get close to the original runtime. If you still get the red flash with a brand-new pack, the problem is in the machine's electronics, and contacting Dyson support would be the next step. That outcome is unlikely given your symptoms.
